source: Markovits, Brisson, de Chantal (2015) Additional evidence for a dual-strategy model of reasoning: probabilistic reasoning is more invariant than reasoning about logical validity (Study 1)
finding: Diagnostic-classified counterexample reasoners and statistical reasoners accept the same logical inferences at first. After 980-of-1000 supporting statistics are added, counterexample reasoners almost stop accepting; statistical reasoners keep accepting.
numbers: N=107 college students (53 counterexample, 30 statistical, 24 other). Accepted of 2, initial to updated: CE 1.51 to 0.13; stat 1.50 to 0.97; other 1.33 to 0.71. Strategy x Inference F(1,74)=15.29, p<.001, partial eta2=.171.
limits: Paper-and-pencil, self-paced, French-speaking Quebec students, one lab. Abstract content ('Kronus' nonsense planet).
agent_relevance: The same evidence (a 98% rate) is read as a reason to accept by one style and as irrelevant (any exception kills validity) by the other. If we ask an agent to judge necessity, we must say which reading we want.

source: Markovits, Brisson, de Chantal (2015) Additional evidence for a dual-strategy model of reasoning: probabilistic reasoning is more invariant than reasoning about logical validity (Study 2)
finding: When the question is explicitly 'how probable is the conclusion', counterexample and statistical reasoners respond alike. The strategy gap exists only for logical-validity judgments.
numbers: N=86 university students (47 CE, 28 stat, 11 other). Mean probability rating initial/updated: CE .789/.775; stat .763/.762. No term involving inference type significant (F<1). Post hoc power 99.9% to detect the Study 1 interaction.
limits: Null result on interaction; power computed post hoc from Study 1 effect size. Probabilistic updating barely rose even with strong evidence (authors flag this as odd).
agent_relevance: Wording of the task instruction, not the person (or model), creates most of the split. A probability-framed prompt should remove strategy variance; a validity-framed prompt exposes it.

source: Markovits, Brisson, de Chantal (2015) Additional evidence for a dual-strategy model of reasoning: probabilistic reasoning is more invariant than reasoning about logical validity (Study 3)
finding: Order effect: doing explicitly probabilistic items first pushes people toward the statistical strategy on later validity items. Doing validity items first does not change later probability ratings.
numbers: N=92. Updated-conclusion acceptance on validity items: 0.96 (SD .88) after probabilistic items vs 0.53 (SD .80) after validity items first. Inference type x Order F(1,89)=4.45, p<.05, eta2p=.048. Probability ratings: no effects; power 95.9%.
limits: Effect size is small (eta2p .048). Between-subject order only, single paper.
agent_relevance: Strategy can be primed by what came before. Order of tasks in a scaffold (probability estimate first, then validity check) could silently bias the validity step toward the statistical reading.

source: Markovits, Brisson, de Chantal (2015) Additional evidence for a dual-strategy model of reasoning: probabilistic reasoning is more invariant than reasoning about logical validity (Study 1 diagnostic design)
finding: The strategy diagnostic: 13 conditional AC items with frequency data. Items give about 10% or about 50% alternative-antecedent rates, plus 3 items at 0%. Reject all of the 10% and 50% items = counterexample. Accept 10% items more than 50% items = statistical. Anything else = other.
numbers: 13 items (5 at ~10%, 5 at ~50%, 3 at 0%); second set repeats with new content. In Study 1: 53 CE (49.5%), 30 stat (28%), 24 other (22%) of 107.
limits: Classification is an arbitrary cut on a short test with no published reliability in this paper; the 'other' group (about a quarter) is excluded from every analysis.
agent_relevance: The diagnostic is itself a usable probe: ask an agent the same 90%/50% items and see whether it rejects all (counterexample-like) or tracks probability (statistical-like).

source: Markovits, Brisson, de Chantal (2015) as summary of Markovits et al. (2013) time-pressure switching and Markovits et al. (2012) diagnostic
finding: As summarised in the 2015 paper: under time pressure people lean statistical on validity judgments; with more time they lean counterexample. This is used to argue the strategies are two modes available to one person, not only fixed types.
numbers: Second-hand: no Ns or effect sizes given in the summary I read. Original (Markovits, Brunet, Thompson, Brisson 2013) not opened.
quote: reasoners ... will preferentially use a statistical strategy when they are time-constrained, but will change to a counterexample strategy when allowed more time
limits: Secondary description only. Same paper also says a statistical strategy need not be cheap in principle; only the empirical pattern suggests it.
agent_relevance: Time or token budget is a lever that may move an agent's strategy. Short budget leads to plausibility-style answers; long budget leads to exception search.

source: de Chantal, Newman, Thompson, Markovits (2020) Who resists belief-biased inferences? Reasoning strategies, working memory, and attentional focus (Study 1 classification)
finding: With 139 adults, 45% classify as statistical, 31% as counterexample, 24% as other. Strategy is a strong individual-difference variable in a general adult sample.
numbers: N=139 (ages 18-49). Statistical 62 (45%), counterexample 43 (31%), other 34 (24%). Statistical = 10% acceptances minus 50% acceptances >= 2. Continuous score correlated r=.97 with the dichotomy.
limits: Base rates differ by sample: here statistical is the largest group; in the 2,122-person Prolific sample counterexample and statistical were about equal (see b19). 28 more dropped for WM accuracy rule.
agent_relevance: Do not assume a default strategy base rate. Expect roughly one third of reasoners (and possibly of sampled model outputs) to hold to exception-search under validity framing.

source: de Chantal, Newman, Thompson, Markovits (2020) Who resists belief-biased inferences? Reasoning strategies, working memory, and attentional focus (Study 1 accuracy and WM)
finding: Counterexample reasoners give far more logically correct answers on belief-conflict syllogisms. The strategy effect is separate from working memory and larger than it.
numbers: n=66 after WM exclusions. Correct overall CE .82 vs stat .56; conflict problems CE .76 vs stat .32; no reliable difference on non-conflict. Strategy x type F(1,64)=19.90, eta2p=.237. Regression on belief score: R=.53, 27.7% variance; strategy beta=-.42 (p<.001); WM beta=-.21 (p=.07). WM alone 10.9%; strategy adds 15.5%; strategy alone 23.7%.
limits: Analysed sample was only 47.5% of those tested after a priori WM exclusions (authors say full-sample continuous analysis gave identical results). Correlational. Counterexample reasoners also had higher WM.
agent_relevance: Resisting belief-bias is mostly about which search procedure runs, not raw capacity. Supports forcing an explicit exception-search step rather than just giving more thinking room.

source: de Chantal, Newman, Thompson, Markovits (2020) Who resists belief-biased inferences? Reasoning strategies, working memory, and attentional focus (Study 2 eye tracking)
finding: Eye tracking shows the process difference: on conflict syllogisms counterexample reasoners look longer at the premises. No difference on non-conflict problems.
numbers: N=196 tested; df of 111 in t tests implies about 113 classified. Conflict problems: CE longer fixation on premises (Welch t test); non-conflict t(111) not significant. Exact t values not captured in my extraction.
limits: Exact statistics not captured; fixation times are a proxy for attention to counterexample-relevant information. Statistical reasoners also slowed on conflict, but less.
agent_relevance: Counterexample strategy looks like re-reading the premises when a conflict is detected. An agent analogue: re-quote and re-check premises only when belief and form disagree (consistent with schema G1).

source: Markovits, Brisson, de Chantal, Thompson (2017) Interactions between inferential strategies and belief bias (Study 1)
finding: Statistical reasoners show a much larger effect of conclusion belief on accepting invalid syllogism conclusions. Counterexample reasoners show a smaller but still real belief effect.
numbers: 170 classified (87 CE, 83 stat; plus 61 other). Belief effect (believable minus unbelievable acceptances out of 4): stat M=2.47, t(82)=15.08, d=1.66; CE M=1.47, t(86)=9.66, d=1.04. Strategy x Problem type F(1,168)=19.92, eta2p=.106; strategy main effect eta2p=.150. Task order: no effect (chi2(2)=3.42), though statistical was somewhat more frequent when the belief task came first (47 vs 36 stat; 37 vs 50 CE).
limits: Counterexample strategy reduces belief bias but does not remove it (d=1.04 is still large). Study 1 order trend is non-significant.
agent_relevance: Counterexample-style search lowers the belief effect (d 1.66 to 1.04) but never to zero. Never claim an exception-search step eliminates belief effects.

source: Markovits, Brisson, de Chantal, Thompson (2017) Interactions between inferential strategies and belief bias (Studies 2-3 generalisation, speed, feeling of rightness)
finding: The belief-by-strategy interaction replicates with valid syllogisms and with some/all syllogisms across three studies. Statistical reasoners are faster. Both groups show the same pattern of slowdown and lower feeling of rightness (FOR) on conflict problems.
numbers: Interaction tests across later studies: F(1,153)=16.16; F(1,99)=7.23; F(1,99)=5.56; F(1,101)=9.02 (assignment of each F to Study 2 or 3 not verified). Ns for Studies 2-3 not captured.
limits: Both groups seem to detect the conflict (similar RT and FOR patterns), so the difference is in what they do with the conflict, not in noticing it.
agent_relevance: Conflict detection is common to both strategies; resolution is the divider. A scaffold should invest in resolution (go find the exception) rather than detection.

source: Markovits, de Chantal, Brisson, Dube, Thompson, Newman (2021) Reasoning strategies predict use of very fast logical reasoning (Study 1: 3.5 s and 5 s limits)
finding: Even under severe time limits counterexample reasoners are better at rejecting invalid inferences (AC) and nonsense non-sequiturs. Statistical reasoners fall to chance on non-sequiturs at 3.5 s.
numbers: 3.5 s group: 44 CE, 32 stat, 25 other; 5 s group: 41 CE, 30 stat, 34 other. Non-sequitur rejection: CE .84 vs stat .60 overall; at 3.5 s stat .503 (chance) vs CE .76; at 5 s CE .92, stat .66. AC correct: CE .59 vs stat .31; valid AA .94 for both. Form x Strategy eta2p=.151; time effect eta2p=.060 (nonlogical), .031 (AA/AC).
limits: Rapid judgment is about very simple forms. Missing responses 0% at 5 s, 1.6% at 3.5 s. Online sample.
agent_relevance: The counterexample style is not just slower; it is more accurate on invalid forms even when rushed. A 'fast' mode that still blocks affirming the consequent is possible if the check is cheap and form-based.

source: Markovits, de Chantal, Brisson, Dube, Thompson, Newman (2021) Reasoning strategies predict use of very fast logical reasoning (Study 2: WM and strategy under a 4 s limit)
finding: Under a 4 s limit working memory stops predicting performance on AC and non-sequitur items while strategy still does. With unlimited time both matter.
numbers: Time x form: time hurt AC and nonlogical, not AA (F(1,288)=15.75). Regression on non-sequitur items: R2 33.6%; strategy b=0.13 (p<.01); WM b=.02 (p<.001); WM x condition b=-.02 (p<.05). Unlimited time: WM b=.02 (p=.002), strategy b=.13 (p=.026). Limited time: no appreciable WM effect.
limits: Strategy evidence for non-sequiturs under time limit was 'weak' per the authors; stronger for AC forms.
agent_relevance: Capacity is the wrong thing to give an agent under a tight budget; a good procedure is. Argues for compact rules (fixed check list) over big context.

source: Markovits, de Chantal, Brisson, Dube, Thompson, Newman (2021) Reasoning strategies predict use of very fast logical reasoning (Study 3: IQ control)
finding: Strategy use predicts logical answers on belief-conflict syllogisms under a 4 s limit even after controlling fluid intelligence (Raven short form). Raven does not.
numbers: N=150: 43 CE, 56 stat, 51 other. Conflict correct .27 (vs .51 unlimited time in prior study); consistent .74 (vs .84). Strategy-Raven r(99)=.33; Raven CE 7.09 vs stat 5.38 (of 12). Regression R2=18.8%; only strategy significant (b=0.23, t(94)=4.16, p<.0001).
limits: Strategy and IQ are correlated (r=.33), so strategy may partly proxy ability. 14.3% missing responses.
agent_relevance: Procedure beats general ability as predictor for quick belief-conflict tasks. The lever to pull is the method, not model size alone.

source: Brisson and Markovits (2020) Reasoning strategies and semantic memory effects in deductive reasoning (Study 1)
finding: Strategy matters only for the invalid forms (AC, DA). Counterexample reasoners endorse invalid conclusions less often; MP and MT show no strategy effect. This holds over and above the classic number-of-alternatives effect.
numbers: N=104 (47 CE, 38 stat, 19 other excluded). Invalid conclusions endorsed (of 3): CE M=0.99 vs stat M=1.55. Validity x Strategy F(1,77)=10.5, eta2p=.118. Premise-type (few vs many alternatives) F(1,77)=16.42, eta2p=.176. Strategy effect on MP/MT: none.
limits: Many vs few alternatives is a content effect that works in both strategies; strategy shifts the threshold, not the retrieval.
agent_relevance: Both styles retrieve the same alternatives; the difference is what they do with them (reject on any vs weigh them). Fits the model: counterexample = a 'one found, reject' rule; statistical = a likelihood sum.

source: Brisson and Markovits (2020) Reasoning strategies and semantic memory effects in deductive reasoning (Study 2, incompatibility statements)
finding: The strategy effect extends to reasoning from 'A and B cannot both be true' statements. Counterexample reasoners endorse the denial inference less often.
numbers: Table 4: Deny-first endorsements (of 4) CE 1.27 (SD 1.72) vs stat 2.11 (SD 1.71); Affirm CE 3.85 vs stat 3.54. Ns for Study 2 not captured.
limits: Smaller-scale extension.
agent_relevance: Same pattern across logical sentence types suggests the strategy is a general stance, not a quirk of if-then.

source: Brisson and Markovits (2020) Reasoning strategies and semantic memory effects in deductive reasoning (Study 3, probabilistic instruction)
finding: With explicit probability ratings the strategy gap disappears: the ratings are similar, so the difference lies in how a likelihood is turned into a yes/no validity decision.
numbers: N=157. Mean likelihood: AC CE 61.2 vs stat 58.0; DA CE 69.9 vs stat 64.5; MP 93.3 vs 87.4; MT 84.9 vs 70.8 (SD about 11-27). Authors report no strategy effect under probabilistic instruction.
limits: MT shows a visible gap in means (84.9 vs 70.8) that the authors do not treat as a strategy effect.
agent_relevance: The threshold, not the belief, is what differs. A scaffold could expose the threshold as a parameter: 'reject if any credible counterexample exists' vs 'accept if likelihood above x'.

source: Markovits, Lortie Forgues, Brunet (2010) Conditional reasoning, frequency of counterexamples, and the effect of response modality
finding: Response format changes the processing mode. Scaled certainty ratings show graded sensitivity to the frequency of exceptions; dichotomous 'follows logically' answers show a different profile, and good abstract reasoners differ only in the categorical condition.
numbers: Study 1: categorical n=70, scaled n=68. Percent accept (MP+MT): no exceptions 87.1; 10% exceptions 38.6 and 34.3; 50% exceptions 32.1 and 28.6. Scaled ratings replicate Geiger and Oberauer (2007): sensitive to frequency (F(1,66)=23.63), not to number of disablers. Study 2 categorical acceptance E0 .92, E10 .45, E50 .09 vs scaled E0 .92, E10 .69, E50 .33.
limits: Earlier (pre-diagnostic) study that motivates the dual-strategy line. Scale numbers in the text extraction are partly garbled.
agent_relevance: Do not elicit a confidence rating and a validity verdict in the same breath if you want the verdict to be independent. A graded number pushes toward the statistical mode.

source: Markovits et al. (2021) Reasoning strategies determine the effect of disconfirmation on belief in false claims (disconfirmation effect)
finding: With 2,122 people, a single disconfirming case reduces belief a bit more for counterexample reasoners than for statistical reasoners. The interaction is tiny.
numbers: Condition x Strategy F(1,1290)=5.57, p=.018, eta2p=.004. Disconfirmation condition main effect eta2p=.112; baseline belief: no strategy effect (CE 1.57 vs stat 0.71, F=1.2). Three-way with number of repetitions p=.074.
limits: Very small effect, p=.018, not corrected for the many tests in the model. Repetition raised belief in both groups as hypothesised.
agent_relevance: Evidence that the strategy split shows up outside deduction, but effect sizes shrink away from the diagnostic's home task. Treat strategy as a modest knob, not a master switch.

source: Markovits et al. (2021) Reasoning strategies determine the effect of disconfirmation on belief in false claims (base rates)
finding: Population mix in a large general sample: about one third counterexample, one third statistical, one quarter unclassifiable. The authors cite Thompson and Markovits (2021): 'other' is made of strategy switchers and people who misunderstood the task.
limits: 'Other' is not a strategy; excluding it removes about a quarter of people from each study and may inflate the apparent separation.
agent_relevance: If strategy mixes are mostly consistent but a quarter switch, an agent also needs a switching rule, not only two modes.

source: Beghin and Markovits (2022) Reasoning strategies and prior knowledge effects in contingency learning
finding: In causal-judgment tasks statistical reasoners give higher causal strength ratings than counterexample reasoners, independent of how plausible the cause is and of the data. The strategy effect holds in a task with no logical-validity question.
numbers: Study 1: strategy F(1,124)=4.61, p=.034, eta2p=.036 (stat M=48.2 vs CE 40.8); plausibility eta2p=.106. Study 2: strategy F(1,298)=11.84, p=.001, eta2p=.038 (stat 51.6); plausibility eta2p=.078; sufficiency eta2p=.157. No strategy x plausibility interaction.
limits: Effect sizes are small (eta2p about .04) and the strategy effect is about conservatism, not accuracy. Authors tie it to sufficiency vs necessity weighting, from earlier work.
agent_relevance: Generalises the claim: counterexample-style means more conservative and attends to necessity (cases where the effect occurs without the cause). A usable tilt toward caution in causal claims.

source: Beeson, Stupple, Schofield, Staples (2019) Mental Models or Probabilistic Reasoning or Both (Psychological Topics 28(1)) (strategy selection)
finding: Review of the dual-strategy model: whether strategy choice is deliberate is open. The least demanding strategy tends to be chosen (Beilock and DeCaro 2007); Roberts (2000) argued people switch strategy between tasks or trials; some in the diagnostic show weak preferences and may be switchers.
numbers: Review, no new data. Names missing work: monitoring and control (meta-reasoning) processes that select the strategy; whether choice is volitional or implicit is unresolved.
limits: Authors state that further research on strategy selection is needed; nothing here directly tests volitional choice.
agent_relevance: Honest summary for the agent designer: no experiment shows people can instruct themselves into a strategy; the evidence is only that time and response format shift it. Treat deliberate selection as a design hypothesis [D], not a finding.

source: Beeson, Stupple, Schofield, Staples (2019) Mental Models or Probabilistic Reasoning or Both (Psychological Topics 28(1)) (MMT and PHM as specifications; criticisms)
finding: Proposes mental models theory as the counterexample strategy's specification and the Probability Heuristics Model (min-heuristic etc.) as the statistical one. Notes PHM problems: 'no valid conclusion' responses are poorly explained (Hattori 2016); a counterexample strategy can explain those; syllogism figure should affect counterexample but not PHM reasoners.
numbers: Untested prediction offered: non-contiguous middle-term figures harder only for counterexample reasoners (Stupple and Ball 2007). Min-conclusions give stronger feeling of rightness and are reassessed less often.
limits: The mapping to MMT and PHM is a proposal in this review, not tested; the original model (Verschueren et al. 2005) was minimalist.
agent_relevance: Competing theories are being turned into strategies rather than rivals. Our schema can hold both: exception search for necessity claims, probability heuristics (min, attachment) as a fast fallback.

source: Beeson, Stupple, Schofield, Staples (2019) Mental Models or Probabilistic Reasoning or Both (Psychological Topics 28(1)) (individual differences and soft normativism)
finding: Predicts statistical reasoners may be 'cognitive misers' with lower WM, or fail to decouple; notes that someone who reads the task as a plausibility judgement rather than logical necessity can reasonably use a statistical strategy (soft normativism).
numbers: Hypotheses only. Partly supported later (CE have higher WM and Raven; see b07, b13) but moderate (Raven r=.33).
limits: Prediction partly supported with moderate correlations only.
agent_relevance: Instruction wording is part of the task: 'must follow' vs 'is likely'. Put the intended norm in the instruction explicitly.

source: Markovits, Brisson, de Chantal, Singmann (2018) as summarised in Beeson et al. (2019): dual-source plus dual-strategy
finding: As summarised by Beeson et al.: logical form influences deductive inference equally for counterexample and statistical reasoners, and also influences probabilistic inferences with explicit statistics, but less clearly.
numbers: Second-hand; no figures given. Original not opened.
limits: Secondary description.
agent_relevance: Form cues (affirming vs denying) act as a separate intuition stream from belief; strategy does not remove it. Keep form checks independent of belief checks.

source: Knauff and Gazzo Castaneda (2025) Reasoning beyond clicks: disentangling counterexamples and probabilities in conditional reasoning (Exp. 1)
finding: With free-text answers rather than scales, about 30% of answers are fully certain, 42% explain uncertainty by a concrete counterexample, and about 29% by probability. The authors argue rating scales mask counterexample reasoning ('probabilistic masking').
numbers: Exp 1 N=20 (24 inferences each; MP and AC): certain 29.6%, counterexample 41.9%, probability 28.5%. High-probability conditionals: certain 45.3%, counterexample 38.0%, prob 16.6%; low: certain 13.9%, counterexample 45.6%, prob 40.3%. Counterexample > probability significant only for high-probability items (Wilcoxon z=2.09, p=.036).
limits: Small convenience sample, hand coding with predefined categories (rater agreement 98.31% in Exp 2). Challenges the idea that probability dominates but also complicates the Markovits classification.
agent_relevance: A rival read to the dual-strategy 'types': both modes appear within one person, and which is verbalised depends on the probability of the item. Another reason to treat strategy as a state the scaffold can set, not a trait.

source: Knauff and Gazzo Castaneda (2025) Reasoning beyond clicks (Exp. 2)
finding: Dropping the explicit if-then premise does not reduce certainty; the pattern becomes more pronounced. Counterexample-based uncertainty beats probability-based across all problem types.
numbers: Exp 2 N=37. Certain 30.7%, counterexample 45.9%, probability 23.5%. Low-probability items: certain 17.1%, CE 48.0%, prob 34.9%; high: certain 44.2%, CE 43.7%, prob 12.0%. Certain vs uncertain z=3.61, p<.001; counterexample vs prob z=2.94, p=.003.
limits: Still small N; open responses are harder to score. Coding categories were predefined by the authors.
agent_relevance: Probability talk rises when the item truly has a lower chance; exception talk is steady. An agent that writes its reasoning freely will show both.

source: Markovits et al. (2019) The development of fast and slow inferential responding: evidence for a parallel developmental pattern
finding: Adults and 8-10-year-olds show the same combination of rule-based and belief-based cues in fast responses; time limits hurt both cue types differently. Authors read the parallel development as two simultaneous processes, consistent with the dual-strategy model.
numbers: No effect sizes extracted; I read the abstract and introduction only.
limits: Support for dual-strategy specifically is by interpretation; paper is mainly about dual-process timing.
agent_relevance: Rule-based and belief-based signals are both fast in humans, so 'fast equals heuristic' is the wrong mental model for our scaffold; a fast pass can be logic-aware.

source: Verschueren, Schaeken, d'Ydewalle (2005) original dual-strategy papers (Thinking and Reasoning 11(3); Memory and Cognition 33(1))
finding: Original proposal as described by every later paper: counterexample strategy is higher in working memory cost and more variable; statistical strategy is cheap and intuitive. Beeson et al. call the original statistical strategy minimalist.
numbers: Not available to me; cited descriptions only.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Origin of the claim that counterexample search costs working memory; later work (b12) shows the cost matters mainly with unlimited time.

source: Markovits, Lortie-Forgues, Brunet (2012) More evidence for a dual-process model of conditional reasoning
finding: Introduced the diagnostic that splits reasoners by whether they reject conclusions regardless of stated probability or follow the stated probability (as described in later papers).
numbers: Not opened; later papers (b04, b06) give the scoring rule.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: The diagnostic items are few and could be given to the agent as a probe.

source: Thompson and Markovits (2020/2021) strategy versus cognitive capacity; cited in b11 and b19
finding: Cited as showing fluid intelligence and strategy each predict choosing the logical response on belief-conflict items, and that the 'other' diagnostic category consists of switchers and people who misunderstood the task.
numbers: Not opened. Figures not seen.
limits: Second-hand through b11 and b19.
agent_relevance: If it holds, strategy and ability are separate dials, so a stronger model alone does not substitute for a counterexample step.

source: Markovits et al. (2025) The impact of counterexample-based training on fast and slow reasoning with familiar content (OSF registration)
finding: Only a title was found. A training study targeting the counterexample strategy exists on OSF; no result known to me.
numbers: None seen.
limits: I did not open the page. No evidence yet that training changes strategy.
agent_relevance: Our scaffold could be a clean test of an instruction-induced counterexample strategy.
